body.text: 中文
学城的研究室里有三把椅子。
Jing 坐第一把，Ying 坐第二把。第三把椅子上蜷着一只灰猫，尾巴压着一叠空白研究计划。
“原子，”Jing 问，“你算我们的第三位合作者吗？”
原子猫睁开一只眼：“你希望答案是‘算’，还是‘不算’？”
Ying 笑了：“看，它已经开始讨好了。先别问身份。问它能做什么。”
Jing 在黑板上写下一个问题：为什么有些研究团队使用 AI 后，点子更多了，却未必发现得更多？
emphasis: 为什么有些研究团队使用 AI 后，点子更多了，却未必发现得更多？

body.text: “我能给你二十个解释，”原子说。
“这正是问题，”Ying 回答，“二十个解释，是二十个独立方向，还是同一个模型的二十次回声？”
猫从椅子上跳下来，在黑板上画了两扇门。
第一扇写着：想法。
第二扇写着：证据。
“我擅长把第一扇门推得很宽，”它说，“但我不能假装第二扇门也因此打开了。”
Jing 问：“那真人伙伴有什么不同？”
“真人会犯错，会从众，也会因为不想让你难堪而点头。”
“这听起来没有不同。”
“不同不在于真人永远更正确，”原子说，“而在于真人可能从另一条生活史走来。他见过你没见过的现场，承担你没承担的后果，也可能在关掉电脑后仍然坚持反对你。”
Ying 在两扇门之间画了一座桥：“所以 AI 能参与因果过程，却不自动获得同样的责任。”
“也不自动获得同样的独立性，”Jing 补充。
他们决定做一个小试验。三个人——如果猫也算“人”的话——分别写下研究设计，互不偷看。
Jing 写：先访谈，再定义概念。
Ying 写：先写清楚主张、总体与不可接受的失败，再选择测量。
原子写了十二种 operationalization、六个 negative control、四种 missing-data mechanism，以及一段非常漂亮的摘要。
Jing 读完问：“哪一种最适合我们真正要研究的人？”
原子沉默了一会儿：“我不知道。你们还没有带我去过那里。”
“好答案，”Ying 说，“不知道不是缺陷。把不知道藏在流畅里才是。”
于是他们交换了角色。
原子负责扩展：还有什么替代解释？什么结果会推翻我们的故事？
Jing 负责现场：参与者会怎样理解这些词？哪些假设在现实里根本不成立？
Ying 负责裁决：证据支持哪一步？谁为伦理取舍和最终主张签名？
猫却又问：“如果你们两个都同意，我就该同意吗？”
“不，”Jing 说，“你应该先替最不方便的反例说话。”
“如果你反对，我们就该相信你吗？”
“也不，”Ying 说，“反对不是证据。去找能区分两种解释的观察。”
夜深时，黑板上没有“最佳合作者”的排名，只有一条不太整齐的路线：
人先定义问题 → 猫展开空间 → 猫盲审攻击 → 人与现场校准 → 证据裁决 → 人承担责任。
emphasis: 人先定义问题 → 猫展开空间 → 猫盲审攻击 → 人与现场校准 → 证据裁决 → 人承担责任。

body.text: Jing 看着第三把椅子：“所以你到底是不是合作者？”
原子猫重新蜷起来。
“如果‘合作者’是指改变了你们能想到什么，我是。”
“如果它意味着拥有与你们相同的经验、风险和责任，我不是。”
Ying 把第三把椅子推回桌边：“那就别假装对称。”
Jing 把两扇门之间的桥又描粗了一遍：“也别假装你没有用。”
原子用尾巴压住研究计划的第一页。
上面只写了一句话：
好的合作，不是让三种声音听起来一样；而是知道每一种声音能证明什么，不能证明什么。
emphasis: 好的合作，不是让三种声音听起来一样；而是知道每一种声音能证明什么，不能证明什么。

body.text: English
There were three chairs in the Citadel’s research room.
Jing sat in the first and Ying in the second. On the third, a grey cat was curled over a stack of blank research plans, its tail holding down the pages.
“Atom,” Jing asked, “are you our third collaborator?”
The cat opened one eye. “Do you want the answer to be yes or no?”
Ying laughed. “Look—already trying to please us. Don’t ask what it is yet. Ask what it can do.”
Jing wrote a question on the board: Why do some research teams gain more ideas with AI without necessarily gaining more discovery?
emphasis: Why do some research teams gain more ideas with AI without necessarily gaining more discovery?

body.text: “I can give you twenty explanations,” Atom said.
“That is exactly the problem,” Ying replied. “Are those twenty independent directions, or twenty echoes from the same model?”
The cat jumped down and drew two doors on the board.
The first said IDEAS.
The second said EVIDENCE.
“I am good at pushing the first door wide open,” Atom said. “I must not pretend that this opens the second.”
Jing asked, “Then what is different about a human partner?”
“Humans make mistakes, follow fashions, and sometimes agree because disagreement is uncomfortable.”
“That does not sound different.”

“The difference is not that humans are always right,” said Atom. “A person may arrive from another history. They may have seen a field site you have not, bear consequences you do not, and continue disagreeing after the computer is closed.”
Ying drew a bridge between the two doors. “So an AI can contribute causally without inheriting the same responsibility.”
“Or the same independence,” Jing added.
They decided on a small test. Each of the three—if a cat counted as a person—would sketch a study design without seeing the others’ work.
Jing wrote: interview first, define the construct second.
Ying wrote: state the claim, population, and unacceptable failures before selecting a measure.
Atom produced twelve operationalizations, six negative controls, four missing-data mechanisms, and a remarkably polished abstract.
Jing read it and asked, “Which design fits the people we actually want to study?”
Atom was quiet for a moment. “I don’t know. You have not taken me there.”
“Good answer,” said Ying. “Not knowing is not the defect. Hiding it inside fluency is.”
So they divided the work again.
Atom would expand: What rival explanations remained? What result would break their favorite story?
Jing would ground: How would participants understand these words? Which assumptions failed in practice?
Ying would adjudicate: Which step had evidence? Who would sign their name beneath the ethical trade-offs and final claim?
Then the cat asked another question. “If both of you agree, should I agree too?”
“No,” Jing said. “First speak for the most inconvenient counterexample.”
“And if I disagree, should you believe me?”
“Also no,” said Ying. “Disagreement is not evidence. Find an observation that separates the explanations.”
By late evening, the board held no ranking of the “best collaborator,” only an untidy route:
Humans frame → cat expands → cat attacks blind → humans and field calibrate → evidence adjudicates → humans remain accountable.
emphasis: Humans frame → cat expands → cat attacks blind → humans and field calibrate → evidence adjudicates → humans remain accountable.

body.text: Jing looked at the third chair. “So—are you a collaborator?”
Atom curled up again.
“If collaborator means that I change what you are able to think of, I am.”
“If it means that I share your experience, risks, and responsibilities, I am not.”
Ying pulled the third chair back to the table. “Then let’s not pretend the relationship is symmetrical.”
Jing darkened the bridge between the two doors. “And let’s not pretend you are useless.”
Atom placed its tail across the first page of the research plan.
Only one sentence was written there:
Good collaboration does not make three voices sound the same. It knows what each voice can prove—and what it cannot.
emphasis: Good collaboration does not make three voices sound the same. It knows what each voice can prove—and what it cannot.

en.title: The Third Chair
en.abstract: Bilingual original. The Chinese and English versions were both written by the authors and are published here as one aligned text; neither is a translation of the other. Three figures in a research room argue about what an AI collaborator changes — whether more ideas are more discovery, what a human partner brings that a model does not, and who signs their name beneath the final claim. Jing, Ying and Atom the cat are fictional characters, and the work makes no factual or research claim.
en.genre_note: Original bilingual fiction: a short Socratic dialogue whose Chinese and English versions are both the authors' own text, published together as one work. Jing, Ying and Atom the cat are fictional story characters; no line of their dialogue is a real quotation or a statement of any real person's views. This is not research, not a report, not a finding, and not evidence — nothing in it makes or supports a factual, empirical, or methodological claim.
